title.title: Delocalization in three dimensions, localization in two
title.subtitle: Claim: weak disorder leaves a.c. spectrum on $\mathbb Z^d$, $d \ge 3$; on $\mathbb Z^2$ any disorder gives pure point spectrum

beats.text: Schematic: where an electron's wave sits in a random lattice
Claim: in $d \ge 3$ at weak disorder, some states stay extended (a.c. spectrum)
and in two dimensions any disorder traps every state (pure point spectrum)

achievement.label: Anderson (1958); Simon's extended-states problem (2000)
statement: d \ge 3,\ \text{weak disorder: purely a.c. on an interval}
achievement.context: Before: a.c. spectrum known only on trees; 2D localization only near band edges
achievement.note: Uniform single-site law only; 171 pages, nothing formal on the headline

verify.detail: Lean: only that the almost-sure spectrum on $\mathbb Z^2$ is $[-4-h, 4+h]$, a textbook fact
verify.ourCheck: We compared the Lean scope with the claim; we did not build it

sources.quote: identifying the almost-sure spectrum on Z^2 as [-4-h,4+h]

plain: An electron in a messy crystal: in 3D it can still roam freely, in a flat 2D crystal it always gets stuck

steps: Study the random lattice block by block, at growing scales
Flag uncertain sites and retry them with fresh randomness
Keep their effect small, so waves still spread in 3D
In 2D, a separate uniform estimate traps every state

voice.text: In three dimensions weak disorder leaves waves spread out; in two, any disorder traps them.
Check the lattice block by block, retry uncertain sites, and keep their effect small.
Claimed: both halves of Anderson's picture.
